subject: obstetrics-gynaecology
title: Stages of Labour, Cardinal Movements and the Labour Care Guide

steps.tx: Labour divides into first, second, third and early recovery fourth periods called the **stages of labour**. The first stage dilates the cervix, the second delivers the baby, the third the placenta. Knowing stages structures every labour decision. The fourth stage is the first two hours after the placenta, when most postpartum haemorrhages declare themselves.
steps.say: Stages of labour divide dilation, delivery, placental delivery and recovery periods.

steps.tx: The fetal head does not simply descend; it negotiates. The **cardinal movements** run engagement, descent, flexion, internal rotation, extension, restitution and external rotation as the head adapts its smallest diameters to each pelvic plane. A delay can be located by asking which movement has failed: no flexion suggests a posterior position, no rotation suggests a transverse arrest. That vocabulary turns a vague slow labour into a mechanical problem with named remedies.
steps.say: The cardinal movements are engagement, descent, flexion, rotation, extension and restitution. Locating the failed movement names the remedy in slow labour.

vis.alt: Diagram of the cardinal movements of labour, the fetal head flexing and rotating through the pelvis.
vis.caption: The fetal head is shown flexing and rotating through the pelvic planes during labour. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: The sequence of head movements through the pelvis forms the **cardinal movements**. Engagement, descent, flexion, internal rotation, extension, restitution and external rotation follow in order. Each movement adapts the head to successive pelvic planes. Restitution turns the head back to align with the shoulders, then external rotation shows the shoulders rotating inside.
steps.say: Cardinal movements sequence engagement through external rotation adapting the head to the pelvis.

steps.tx: Passage of the biparietal diameter through the pelvic brim is **engagement**. In first pregnancies it often precedes labour, in later ones it may await contractions. Non engagement with a normal pelvis usually reflects malposition or deflexion. Five fifths to two fifths palpable tracks engagement abdominally, and the finding is written as fifths engaged.
steps.say: Engagement passes the biparietal diameter through the brim, often before labour in first pregnancies.

steps.tx: Progressive downward movement driven by contractions throughout labour is **descent**. It is judged abdominally in fifths and vaginally by station together. Arrest of descent despite good contractions signals obstruction or malposition. Station zero at the spines plus no abdominal fifths felt means the head is well down, and both findings should match.
steps.say: Descent is judged by fifths and station together throughout labour.

steps.tx: Rotation of the occiput to under the pubic arch at the pelvic floor is **internal rotation**. The levator ani gutter directs the head through forty five to ninety degrees. Failure gives deep transverse arrest or persistent posterior position. It is a long internal rotation of 135 degrees from a posterior start, which explains the slower labour.
steps.say: Internal rotation turns the occiput under the pubic arch at the pelvic floor.

steps.tx: The historical graph of expected dilation against time is the **Friedman curve**. Modern data show labour is slower than Friedman taught, especially before six centimetres. Applying old curves caused unnecessary caesareans for normal slow labour. Friedman set one centimetre per hour from 4 centimetres, a line modern data show half of normal women cross.
steps.say: The Friedman curve overstated expected dilation speed compared with modern labour data.

steps.tx: The modern labour chart replaced a ruler with a record of care. The **WHO labour care guide** tracks dilation alongside fetal condition, medicines, fluids and shared decision making, prompting review at set thresholds rather than panic at one line. It accepts slower normal progress than the old partograph did. Its real function is escalation discipline: abnormal observations gathered in one place make the decision to intervene defensible and timely.
steps.say: The WHO labour care guide records dilation with fetal condition, medicines and decisions together. It prompts timely review without the old rigid line.

vis.alt: Image of the WHO labour care guide chart used to monitor labour progress and care.
vis.caption: A labour care guide chart is shown recording progress, fetal condition and care decisions. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: The current WHO intrapartum guide replacing rigid curves with individualised thresholds is the **WHO labour care guide**. It plots progress with supportive care and alert thresholds per parameter. Respectful, woman centred care is built into its design. It sets an alert threshold for each parameter instead of one line for dilation alone.
steps.say: The WHO labour care guide individualises thresholds with respectful woman centred care.

steps.tx: Latent phase up to five centimetres can last many hours normally, termed **prolonged latent phase** tolerance. Admission too early in this phase raises intervention cascades. Reassurance, hydration and analgesia at home or in latent areas serve better. Latent labour can run 20 hours in a first baby without harm when mother and fetus stay well.
steps.say: Prolonged latent phase tolerance avoids intervention cascades from early admission.

steps.tx: Continuous one to one support in labour shortens it and reduces caesareans, an evidence based **support effect**. A chosen companion plus staff presence delivers this benefit cheaply. It is the single most effective non drug labour intervention. Companionship also cuts epidural use, and the benefit holds across income settings in trial data.
steps.say: Continuous support shortens labour and reduces caesareans more than any non drug intervention.
